summary:
Arkhangelsk Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, whose laws set the conditions in force across every region of the country. The sources assembled for this record contain no oblast-specific findings, so the assessment below describes the national climate a visitor to Arkhangelsk enters.

Same-sex activity is not criminalised. Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are banned, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and no discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation or gender identity covers housing, healthcare or employment.

Public expression is itself an offence. 'Gay propaganda' charges carry fines up to 400,000 roubles (about £3,600) for individuals or up to 15 days' detention, and repeat offences can bring criminal prosecution with up to four years in prison. The November 2023 Supreme Court designation of the international LGBT+ movement as an extremist organisation makes participation punishable by two to six years and organising by six to ten years.

The US State Department advises against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, citing the risk of wrongful detention and arbitrary law enforcement.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between December 2022 and March 2024, at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws, and the UK Home Office assesses that trans people, publicly active LGBT+ advocates and those in the North Caucasus are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions tied to the International Public LGBT Movement designation as of 30 June 2025, roughly 98 administrative and three criminal. The Supreme Court ruling of November 2023 entered into force in January 2024 and opened the way to arbitrary prosecutions of LGBT people and their supporters.

Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation; two were sentenced to prison and one died by suicide in pretrial detention. A further 81 people across 98 court cases were found guilty of administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, with fines up to 2,000 roubles, and repeat displays punishable under the criminal code by up to four years.

Charges reach ordinary commercial activity: on 15 May 2025, investigators charged three publishing-house staff under article 282.2 for selling fiction exploring LGBT themes, an offence carrying up to 12 years.
tangentialFactors:
The pace of enforcement has increased alongside its severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million roubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding.

The immediate aftermath of the extremist designation was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which reported a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation. In December 2024 the Associated Press reported that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in housing, healthcare or employment, and legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are unavailable under the 2023 legislation.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

The same UK Home Office note records that at least 139 people were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws between December 2022 and March 2024, and assesses trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates as likely to face persecution.
outOfScopeNotes:
No oblast-level data was sourced for Arkhangelsk Oblast: the UK Home Office note sets national conditions and states that it offers no region-specific findings, and the Human Rights Watch enforcement counts are national tallies not disaggregated by region.

Whether local police or courts in Arkhangelsk Oblast have brought extremism or propaganda cases is unresolved in the sources provided; the named raids, convictions and charges are documented in Moscow, St Petersburg and other locations.

The conversion-therapy case reported by BBC Russian occurred near Novosibirsk and is cited as evidence of documented coercion against transgender people nationally, not as an Arkhangelsk finding.

Local availability of detention facilities, healthcare for trans visitors, and complaint mechanisms in Arkhangelsk Oblast is not sourced here.
